subject: What is the math behind INLA's AR model?

messages.author: 14f33f5ab5b4a1db
messages.subject: What is the math behind INLA's AR model?
parts:
I have specified this AR model with some fixed and random effects:

m1 <- inla(Y~ -1
    + FixedEffect1

    + RandomEffect1

    + f(observation_number, model='ar1',
        replicate=ID,
        values=1:max(df2$ observation_number  ),
        hyper=hyper_AR,
        constr=FALSE
    )
           
    , data=df2, family="gaussian"
    , control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive",  int.strategy="auto")
    , control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE, dic=TRUE, config=TRUE)
    , control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(1/0.01^2))), fixed=TRUE)
    , verbose=TRUE
    )

My coworkers and I are confused as to what value the AR1 term is lagging on. I am assuming that it is lagging on the response variable like in any typical AR definition

Y_t = sum i from 1 to n of rho_i * Y_t-i + epsilon_t

so my AR1 should be Y_t = rho * Y_t-1 + epsilon_t

Some think that the AR term is lagging on the random effects, and not the response variable.

Thank you

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] What is the math behind INLA's AR model?
parts:
No, it doesn’t operate on the response variable directly. It just contributes to the linear predictor. The lags are within the model component. I believe the exact definition is in inla.doc(“ar1”)

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] What is the math behind INLA's AR model?
parts:
Inla deals with additive models, so the connection is that if x is an ar1 process and eps is additive noise (for observation family “gaussian”, and the observations are
Y = x + eps (linear predictor eta = x)
that means y is the sum of an ar1 process and iid noise.

Finn

On 23 Aug 2022, at 22:37, JJ Hubbard <jordanj...@gmail.com> wrote:

﻿ So that doc gives this:

x1 ∼ N (0,(τ (1 − ρ 2 ))−1 ) 
x_i = ρ * x_i−1 + epsilon_i ; epsilon_i ∼ N (0, τ −1 ) i = 2, . . . , n

Which does not depend on any variable from the data since x1 is just a draw from this normal distribution and all future x_1+t values are just multiples of x_t and a learned parameter plus noise. What effect does this try to capture? An AR1 is intuitive to me: I believe that my process at time t is a product of the process value at time t-1 with some parameter to be learned, plus an error term. The specification in INLA does not depend on my Y, nor does it depend on any predictive variable in X, so is it just to account for the error from the individual's previous observation?

On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 1:57:51 PM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
No, it doesn’t operate on the response variable directly. It just contributes to the linear predictor. The lags are within the model component. I believe the exact definition is in inla.doc(“ar1”)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] What is the math behind INLA's AR model?
parts:
When the process is observed with noise, this is a much more natural model than trying to apply the ar1 structure directly onto the observations, since that would mix in the observation noise where it likely doesn’t belong.

Finn

The ar component _is_ one of the structured random effects in the model, so I don’t understand the question.

Finn

On 24 Aug 2022, at 00:13, JJ Hubbard <jordanj...@gmail.com> wrote:

﻿Does this temporal change in the AR1 depend at all on the random effects specified in the model?

On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 4:09:53 PM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
It’s a model component that describes temporal change for each individual.
(“Factor” has a special meaning, so best to avoid that…)

Finn

On 24 Aug 2022, at 00:01, JJ Hubbard <jordanj...@gmail.com> wrote:

﻿So in the replicate model I have specified above, is it fair to think of the AR1 term as some factor that describes an individual? Or is it purely a term to capture any temporal effect?


On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 3:49:56 PM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
When the process is observed with noise, this is a much more natural model than trying to apply the ar1 structure directly onto the observations, since that would mix in the observation noise where it likely doesn’t belong.

Finn

On 23 Aug 2022, at 23:48, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

﻿Inla deals with additive models, so the connection is that if x is an ar1 process and eps is additive noise (for observation family “gaussian”, and the observations are
Y = x + eps (linear predictor eta = x)
that means y is the sum of an ar1 process and iid noise.

Finn

On 23 Aug 2022, at 22:37, JJ Hubbard <jordanj...@gmail.com> wrote:

﻿ So that doc gives this:
x1 ∼ N (0,(τ (1 − ρ 2 ))−1 ) 
x_i = ρ * x_i−1 + epsilon_i ; epsilon_i ∼ N (0, τ −1 ) i = 2, . . . , n

Which does not depend on any variable from the data since x1 is just a draw from this normal distribution and all future x_1+t values are just multiples of x_t and a learned parameter plus noise. What effect does this try to capture? An AR1 is intuitive to me: I believe that my process at time t is a product of the process value at time t-1 with some parameter to be learned, plus an error term. The specification in INLA does not depend on my Y, nor does it depend on any predictive variable in X, so is it just to account for the error from the individual's previous observation?

On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 1:57:51 PM UTC-7 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
No, it doesn’t operate on the response variable directly. It just contributes to the linear predictor. The lags are within the model component. I believe the exact definition is in inla.doc(“ar1”)

Finn

On 23 Aug 2022, at 21:53, JJ Hubbard <jordanj...@gmail.com> wrote:

﻿I have specified this AR model with some fixed and random effects:

m1 <- inla(Y~ -1
    + FixedEffect1

    + RandomEffect1

    + f(observation_number, model='ar1',
        replicate=ID,
        values=1:max(df2$ observation_number  ),
        hyper=hyper_AR,
        constr=FALSE
    )
           
    , data=df2, family="gaussian"
    , control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive",  int.strategy="auto")
    , control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE, dic=TRUE, config=TRUE)
    , control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(1/0.01^2))), fixed=TRUE)
    , verbose=TRUE
    )

My coworkers and I are confused as to what value the AR1 term is lagging on. I am assuming that it is lagging on the response variable like in any typical AR definition

Y_t = sum i from 1 to n of rho_i * Y_t-i + epsilon_t

so my AR1 should be Y_t = rho * Y_t-1 + epsilon_t

Some think that the AR term is lagging on the random effects, and not the response variable.

Thank you
